Ocean target¶

Summary¶

OceanTarget is the sea-surface RCS (Radar Cross-Section) model. Given the bistatic geometry and the carrier wavelength, it returns how strongly the ocean scatters the GNSS signal toward the receiver. It is the ocean side of the link budget – the background that a ship has to stand out from in backscatter mode, and the glint a ship blocks in forward mode.

The model adds two parts:

  • a coherent part – a clean specular reflection off the smooth mean surface (matters only for very calm water);

  • an incoherent part – the diffuse scatter from the rough surface, which is what you usually see. At the specular direction this is the bright “glistening zone”; well off the specular direction (backscatter) it is Bragg scatter from small wind ripples.

It is driven by sea state (wave height, wind speed and direction, water temperature, salinity, wave age), and it uses the building blocks in Ocean physics.

Detailed Module Description¶

The two contributions¶

The total cross-section per sample is the sum

(61)¶\[\sigma = \sigma_\mathrm{coherent} + \sigma_\mathrm{incoherent}.\]

Both use the circular reflectivity \(|R_\mathrm{RL}|^2\) of seawater (the RHCP-to-LHCP power reflectivity from the Klein-Swift permittivity at the carrier frequency, water temperature and salinity).

Coherent (calm-water specular)¶

If the mean sea surface were perfectly smooth, the reflection would be a clean specular one. The cross-section that reproduces that two-ray reflected power through the radar equation is

(62)¶\[\sigma_\mathrm{coherent} = 4\pi\,|R_\mathrm{RL}|^2 \left(\frac{R_t R_r}{R_t + R_r}\right)^2 D^2\, e^{-\kappa},\]

reduced by the Rayleigh roughness loss

(63)¶\[\kappa = \left(\frac{4\pi\,\sigma_h\,\cos\left(\beta/2\right)}{\lambda}\right)^2,\]

where \(\sigma_h\) is RMS surface height, \(\beta\) the bistatic angle (so \(\beta/2\) is the local specular incidence), and \(\lambda\) the wavelength. The configured value is significant wave height \(H_s\); the implementation uses the Gaussian-sea approximation \(\sigma_h \simeq H_s/4\). For normal sea states \(\kappa\) is large and this term collapses to almost nothing; it matters mainly for a very smooth surface. It is applied only where the mean surface is the specular reflector.

The spherical-Earth divergence \(D^2\) accounts for the convex sea surface defocusing the specular bundle relative to a flat mirror:

(64)¶\[D^2 = \left[\left(1 + \frac{2R_\mathrm{red}}{a_e\cos\left(\beta/2\right)}\right) \left(1 + \frac{2R_\mathrm{red}\cos\left(\beta/2\right)}{a_e}\right)\right]^{-1}, \qquad R_\mathrm{red} = \frac{R_t R_r}{R_t + R_r},\]

with mean Earth radius \(a_e\). The two factors are the Coddington astigmatic mirror radii \(a_e\cos\theta\) in the plane of incidence and \(a_e/\cos\theta\) across it; a flat Earth (\(a_e \to \infty\)) recovers \(D = 1\), and grazing incidence drives \(D \to 0\). For a 700 km receiver orbit this costs about 1.7 dB of coherent power. It is exposed in the diagnostics as divergence_factor_sq.

Incoherent (rough surface)¶

The rough surface scatters diffusely. Using geometric optics over the wave-slope statistics, the cross-section per unit area (the NRCS) is

(65)¶\[\sigma^0_\mathrm{GO} = \pi\,|R_\mathrm{RL}|^2 \left(\frac{|\mathbf{q}|}{q_z}\right)^4 P(s_u, s_c),\]

where \(\mathbf{q}\) is the scattering vector (the change in propagation direction), \(q_z\) its part along the surface normal, and \(P(s_u, s_c)\) is the probability of the exact surface slope that would reflect the transmitter into the receiver. Only waves longer than about three radar wavelengths act as specular facets at L band, so \(P\) is a 2-D Gaussian over the large-scale slope variances: the Elfouhaily spectrum integrated up to the two-scale division wavenumber \(k_\mathrm{radar}/3\) (Brown 1978; the same division the two-scale Bragg term uses), split by the Cox-Munk upwind/crosswind anisotropy ratio. Using the full optical Cox-Munk variance would count sub-wavelength ripples as mirrors; at L1 and 7 m/s that understates the glint-peak NRCS by about 3 dB and overstates the off-specular GO skirt. Multiplying by the illuminated area gives the glistening-zone return.

When patch integration is disabled and the footprint contains the complete glint, the implementation uses a peak-equivalent area derived from the local slope-to-surface Jacobian. With reduced range \(R_\mathrm{red}=R_tR_r/(R_t+R_r)\),

(66)¶\[dA=4R_\mathrm{red}^2\,ds_x\,ds_y,\qquad A_\mathrm{eff}=\frac{4R_\mathrm{red}^2}{P(0,0)} =8\pi R_\mathrm{red}^2\sqrt{\sigma_u^2\sigma_c^2}.\]

Thus \(\sigma^0_\mathrm{peak}A_\mathrm{eff}\) preserves the complete first-order geometric-optics integral. If the supplied footprint is smaller, the scalar fallback caps this effective area; patch integration is preferable because it evaluates range, gain and NRCS over the actual footprint.

Bragg backscatter¶

In the backscatter direction at oblique incidence the geometric-optics term collapses (almost no facet is tilted steeply enough to bounce the signal straight back). There the return comes from Bragg resonance with small wind ripples, computed by the two-scale model in Ocean physics. It is switched on only near backscatter (bistatic angle below ~5 deg) and at oblique incidence (at or above 20 deg), so the forward/specular path is left exactly unchanged:

(67)¶\[\text{Bragg active} \iff \beta < 5^\circ \;\text{and}\; \theta_i \ge 20^\circ.\]

The incidence floor is divergence protection, not calibration: first-order Bragg grows without bound toward nadir (\(\sigma^0 \sim B/(4\sin^4\theta)\) as the resonant wavenumber slides into the energetic long-wave spectrum), and the tilt average leaks that growth through mirror-ward-tilted facets well above nadir. Below the gate the quasi-specular geometric-optics term owns the return. Lowering the gate requires first restricting the facet-local Bragg wavenumber inside the tilt average (\(k_B(\theta_\mathrm{local}) \ge k_\mathrm{radar}/3\), the same two-scale division) – a recorded refinement, see TODO.md.

The clutter area¶

This model is area-agnostic: it multiplies an NRCS by whatever illuminated_area_m2 the link budget hands it. That area is the antenna footprint by default, one surface patch under patch integration, or a first-order delay-Doppler cell when that model is on. At exact specular geometry that first-order cell is singular and the current implementation uses the footprint cap, not a small second-order cell.

Module Assumptions and Limitations¶

  • Coherent term gated to specular. The specular reflection is only added where the surface itself is the specular reflector; it is zero off-specular, and collapses for any realistic wave height. Its spherical-Earth divergence uses the mean Earth radius, not the local curvature of the ellipsoid.

  • Hard Bragg gating. Bragg is added only for bistatic angle below 5 deg and incidence at least 20 deg. The incidence floor is divergence protection for the near-nadir blow-up of first-order Bragg (see above), so parameter sweeps show a step at the gate; the smooth facet-local gate that would replace it is a recorded refinement. Out-of-plane polarisation rotation is not included.

  • Sea-state ranges. Wind speed > 0; wave age between 0.84 and 5.0; temperature and salinity in the Klein-Swift range. Out-of-range inputs raise.

  • Area comes from the link budget. The absolute diffuse power depends on the illuminated area supplied from outside (footprint, patch, or DDM cell), not chosen here.

  • Empirical-model scope. The implementation combines Klein-Swift, Cox-Munk, Elfouhaily, geometric optics and a gated two-scale Bragg term. It has not been calibrated end-to-end against a particular GNSS-R instrument or collocated ocean dataset.

Validation and Tests¶

Test group

What it checks

TestOceanTargetConstruction

Inputs validated; from_settings round-trips the [OCEAN] fields.

TestOceanTargetComputeRcs

Coherent term dominates for calm/smooth water and collapses for a rough sea; the coherent term carries the spherical-Earth divergence \(D^2\) (closed-form anchor at rtol \(10^{-12}\)); the glistening area grows with wind and is capped by a supplied illuminated area; the roughness loss grows with wave height, using \(\sigma_h=H_s/4\); the uncapped peak-equivalent area preserves the analytic geometric-optics integral.

TestOceanTargetComputeRcs (Bragg)

Bragg is zero at forward specular and near nadir, dominates at oblique backscatter, and uses the supplied illuminated area.

TestComputeReflectionLinkBudgetIntegration

The default target matches an explicit OceanTarget; a custom target replaces the ocean RCS.

These tests establish equations, limiting cases and broad physical trends. They are not an external cross-validation against CYGNSS, Aquarius, or measured DDMs; see Verification and validation status.

References¶

  • Zavorotny, V. & Voronovich, A., “Scattering of GPS signals from the ocean with wind remote sensing application”, IEEE TGRS 38(2), 2000.

  • Klein, L. & Swift, C., “An improved model for the dielectric constant of sea water at microwave frequencies”, IEEE Trans. Antennas Propag. 25(1), 1977.

  • Cox, C. & Munk, W., “Measurement of the roughness of the sea surface from photographs of the sun’s glitter”, J. Opt. Soc. Am. 44(11), 1954.

  • Brown, G., “Backscattering from a Gaussian-distributed perfectly conducting rough surface”, IEEE Trans. Antennas Propag. 26(3), 1978 (two-scale division wavenumber).

  • Beckmann, P. & Spizzichino, A., The Scattering of Electromagnetic Waves from Rough Surfaces, Pergamon, 1963 (spherical-Earth divergence factor).
